content: I'm just wondering, which of the available tactics will always find the shortest proof? Of those, which will produce the code for the proof to replace its call with?
And which algorithms exist that could do so, but have not been turned into tactics yet?
The clarify, I mean tactics that 'start from scratch', not those that find existing proofs to use.
This topic was moved here from #metaprogramming / tactics > decidable tactics by Paige Thomas.

What do you mean exactly by "shortest proofs"?
If you have a specific measure of proof length, it is in general very hard to know whether any proof is the one that minimizes this measure.
If you mean something more vague, basic "plumbing" tactics like exact, refine and apply generate very short proofs, and automation tactics like simp, grind , linarith, ring tend to generate long proofs.

So in classical propositional logic, using the three axiom schemes and modus ponens, one step in a proof would be an instantiation of one the axiom schemes or an application of modus ponens. In this system I would consider the length of a proof to be the number of these steps. I learned that one can use unification and iterate through these proofs in order of increasing length. So the shortest proof in this case would be found by doing this and stopping at the proof of the theorem being searched for. I would guess the same could be done for natural deduction. I'm wondering if there are similar algorithms for other parts of math, and also if they exist as tactics that will insert the found proof into the file.
I don't know whether it will actually give you the shortest proof term but there's a good chance

and I don't think there are any other tools like this; I mean, most of the time you're not too concerned with the length of the proof and rather that it works at all and how fast it is generated and checked
Hmm. I think I'm just looking for tactics and algorithms that can be guaranteed to give the shortest proof if it exists, for this question anyway.
Interest and an obsession with perfection :) I would probably try to implement the algorithms as tactics if they are not already. Of course I would need to learn how to write tactics to do so...

Hmm I believe canonical is exhaustive so it should be enough (even if it doesn't produce the shortest proof immediately, you can probably tell it to generate sufficiently many solutions to be sure you got the shortest one)

I've played with Canonical before, and it looked cool, although it had a bug that was making it fail on certain goals on the latest Lean version at the time. It may be fixed now, I haven't checked. I think though I'm still focused on ones designed and guaranteed to find the shortest proof if it exists. It doesn't need to be general for any proof, just like, this one works for propositional logic, this one works for linear equalitys, etc.

I think at metamath there was a competition who can find the shortest proof of a proposition based on the axioms a1,a2,a3 and mp. It typically stops at 14 steps or so. Lean proofs are massive but if you reduce yourself to tactics you might find some pretty neat one-liners.
